cards.title: Efficient explicit constant-rate tree codes
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed finite output alphabet \(\Sigma\), constants \(0<\delta<1\) and \(0<\alpha<\delta/2\), and uniform deterministic polynomial-time encoding and decoding algorithms for binary tree codes of every height \(N\ge1\), with relative tree distance at least \(\delta\) and decoding from suffix error fraction at most \(\alpha\)? Both \(|\Sigma|\) and the two positive distance parameters must be independent of \(N\). The binary information rate \(1/\log_2|\Sigma|\) is therefore a positive constant. The precise causal and decoding requirements are specified below.
cards.why: Tree codes protect communication whose later symbols depend on earlier interaction. A constant alphabet and positive tree distance would keep redundancy bounded while maintaining distinguishability after every possible divergence. Efficient deterministic encoding and decoding would supply a central explicit object in the theory of reliable interactive communication.
cards.status_note: The checked May 2026 primary discussion still identifies explicit constant-rate positive-distance tree-code construction as open. Its rate–immediacy bound assumes an extra property absent from this target and does not refute general tree codes. Bounded subsequent-result searches through 2026-09-15 found no unconditional construction or impossibility result for the precise efficient-encoding-and-decoding target here; the review does not certify exhaustive current openness.

progress.text: Wigderson’s draft states Open Problem 15.34, asking for explicit tree codes with efficient encoding and decoding and both rate and distance constant.
Gelles, Haeupler, Kol, Ron-Zewi and Wigderson give a precise suffix-distance definition of efficient decoding and a construction with weaker distance parameters.
The construction by Ben Yaacov, Cohen and Yankovitz has rate \(\Omega(1/\log\log N)\) for constant distance, as described in the checked 2026 primary discussion.
The revised rate–immediacy paper retains the general explicit constant-rate construction problem and proves a bound for a stronger restricted property.

importance.reason: Efficient explicit tree codes would give a fundamental construction for reliable interactive communication.

sentences: A binary tree code assigns output labels to every possible input history as that history unfolds.
After two histories first differ, their output suffixes must disagree on a fixed positive fraction of positions.
A fixed output alphabet keeps the information rate bounded below by a positive constant.
The requested uniform algorithms must encode efficiently and recover any received prefix satisfying the stated suffix-error promise.
The checked 2026 literature still leaves this constant-rate construction open, and its new barrier concerns an additional restricted property.

cards.definitions:
Fix an integer \(q=|\Sigma|\ge2\) and identify \(\Sigma\) with \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), represented by fixed-length binary symbols. For each height \(N\), an encoder defines maps \(C_N:\{0,1\}^{\le N}	o\Sigma^{\le N}\) with \(|C_N(x)|=|x|\), \(C_N(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\), and prefix consistency: if \(u\) is a prefix of \(x\), then \(C_N(u)\) is the prefix of \(C_N(x)\) of length \(|u|\). Thus an output symbol cannot depend on future input bits. For every \(N\ge1\), \(1\le\ell\le N\), and distinct \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}\), let \(j\) be the first input position where \(x_j
e y_j\). The tree-distance requirement is \[ igl|\{t\in\{j,\ldots,\ell\}:C_N(x)_t

e v_t\}|}{\ell-j+1}.\] A decoder receives \(1^N\) and any \(w\in\Sigma^\ell\), \(1\le\ell\le N\), and returns a binary string of length \(\ell\), or a failure symbol. For every \(x\in\{0,1\}^\ell\), if \(d_{\mathrm{sfx}}(w,C_N(x))\le\alpha\), the output must be exactly \(x\). No correctness requirement is imposed outside this promise, but the decoder must still halt within its time bound. The promise bounds errors in every suffix of the received prefix. It is not a bound on total Hamming error alone, which would not separate paths that diverge close to their end. The encoder and decoder are two fixed finite deterministic Turing-machine programs, with constants \(K,k\), each using at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit steps per invocation on valid inputs. Encoding receives \(1^N\) and the currently available input prefix \(x\), and outputs \(C_N(x)\). The known horizon \(N\) is allowed; the code families for distinct horizons need not agree. All preprocessing, symbol calculations and output writes count toward the time bound, and there is no separately supplied table, advice, random seed, oracle or graph of the exponentially large tree. Constants and programs are independent of \(N\), \(\ell\), \(x\) and \(w\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the fixed alphabet, positive constants, uniform encoder and decoder, and proofs of prefix consistency, the distance inequality, the promised decoding guarantee and polynomial bit complexity; or give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such collection exists. An existence proof for labels without efficient encoding and decoding does not fulfill the target. A growing alphabet, vanishing distance or decoding guarantee for selected input histories alone is insufficient. A limitation of an additional property not required above does not refute the stated existence claim.

context_blocks.text: Wigderson’s Open Problem 15.34 explicitly requests efficient encoding and decoding, constant rate and constant relative distance. The card keeps all four requirements and uses the standard finite-height binary-input formulation.

The 2018 interactive-coding paper defines efficient tree-code decoding through suffix distance: a received prefix is decoded when every suffix has sufficiently few errors. This supplies a concrete promise for the otherwise unspecified decoding clause in the source question.

The checked May 2026 version of Cohen, Schulman and Srivastava records that constant-rate positive-distance tree codes exist nonconstructively, while the explicit constructions discussed there achieve rate \(\Omega(1/\log\log N)\) at constant distance. That rate tends to zero as the horizon grows.

Their rate–immediacy theorem rules out constant rate for codes satisfying an additional immediacy property under the theorem’s hypotheses. General tree codes need not satisfy that property, so the result does not prove impossibility of the encoder and decoder requested here.

Defined a fixed output alphabet and correct binary bit-rate, causal finite-height encodings, input-divergence tree distance, one uniform polynomial bit-time encoder/decoder and all-prefix guarantees. methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
